title: Fixing externalities: taxes, property rights, and Coase
hook: A factory can overshoot by 20 units and nobody in the market notices. Two very different fixes: price the harm, or let the neighbors negotiate.
objectives: Locate the market output and the social optimum, and measure the deadweight loss between them.
Set a Pigouvian tax at marginal damage at Q_FB, and compute who receives the revenue.
Explain why Coase's bargaining reaches the same output under either property-right assignment, and name the three ways it breaks.

blocks.md:
> "This is the most important lecture of the entire course."

A firm picks output where its marginal profit hits zero: **Q_M = 60**. But its neighbor suffers damage that grows with output. Society wants the point where the firm's marginal profit equals the neighbor's marginal damage: **Q_FB = 40**, the *first best*.

Between 40 and 60, each unit costs the neighbor more than it earns the firm. That shaded triangle is the deadweight loss. (The professor's Q* is the free-market output; we call it Q_M here.)

blocks.title: The externality and the social optimum
blocks.caption: Illustrative numbers: MB = 60 - Q, MD = 0.5Q. Dot: social optimum (40, $20). Takeaway: the market keeps producing until profit hits zero, long after the neighbor's pain exceeds it.

blocks.text: Market failure here is a quantity problem: output of 60 instead of 40. Area DWL = 1/2 x 20 x 30 = 300.

blocks.q: At Q = 60 the firm's marginal profit is $0 and marginal damage is $30. Why is 60 too much?
options: Extra units cost the neighbor more than they earn
The firm is losing money on every unit it sells
The neighbor would rather the firm shut down entirely
Marginal damage always exceeds marginal profit, at any output
blocks.why: At Q = 60 an extra unit adds $0 to profit and $30 to damage, so cutting back raises total surplus. Zero output is not optimal either: at Q = 0 marginal profit is $60 and damage is $0.

blocks.md:
To fix this, make the firm feel the damage. Charge a per-unit tax **τ = D′(Q_FB)**: the marginal damage *at the efficient output*. Here τ = 0.5 x 40 = **$20**.

The firm just maximizes profit minus τ·Q and lands on Q_FB by itself. No quota, no calculation on its side.

> "The Pigouvian tax is really just turning the externality into something that's not an externality."

frames.title: Before the tax
frames.text: The firm maximizes profit. Its first-order condition ignores the neighbor.

frames.title: Add one column to the spreadsheet
frames.text: For every unit it produces, the firm pays τ. In the professor's words, it's just another column in the Excel spreadsheet.

frames.title: Set the price of harm
frames.text: The new first-order condition matches the social planner's exactly when τ equals marginal damage.

blocks.title: A tax of $20 puts the firm at Q_FB
blocks.caption: The firm stops where MB meets the tax line, at Q = 40. It gives up 1/2 x 20 x 20 = 200 of profit, but the neighbor avoids 500 of damage (net +300 = the old DWL). Takeaway: the tax's cost is real but dominated by the benefit.

steps.title: Where you set the tax matters

blocks.md:
The marginal damage curve slopes upward, so *where* you read it matters. Reading it at the free-market output gives D′(60) = **$30**, which is too high.

Drag the tax and watch output (Q = 60 - τ) and deadweight loss. At τ = 20 the loss is zero. The professor's warning: set τ = D′(Q_M) and the firm "will pull it back farther than we want it to."

blocks.title: Too high: τ = D′(Q_M) = 30
blocks.caption: Output falls to 30, below Q_FB. Area = 1/2 x 10 x 15 = 75. Takeaway: a tax at the wrong point trades one deadweight loss for a smaller one.

steps.title: Where does the tax money go?

blocks.md:
Unlike a quota, a tax raises money: **R = τ·Q_FB = D′(Q_FB)·Q_FB = 20 x 40 = 800**. That rectangle splits into the neighbor's total damage (400) and the part above it (400).

Revenue can go to the neighbor, the firm, or anyone. One rule: it must preserve incentives.

> "We can write the firm a check for any amount of money. But what's critical is that the firm doesn't believe that what it does will affect what's on the check."

blocks.title: Revenue R = 20 x 40 = 800
blocks.caption: Because MD slopes upward, D′(Q_FB)·Q_FB always exceeds total damage D(Q_FB). Takeaway: hand all the revenue to the neighbor and they end up better off than if the firm never existed.

blocks.title: Who ends up with what (illustrative payoffs)
blocks.caption: Firm profit at Q = 40 is 1600; the tax takes 800. Even with a full lump-sum check the firm sits 200 below its free-market 1800, which is the cost of being distorted.

blocks.q: The firm complains about the tax. Which compensation keeps Q at 40?
options: Refund τ to the firm for every unit it produces
A fixed check sized to its pre-policy output
A check that grows with how much the firm produces
Rebate the tax in proportion to the firm's sales
blocks.why: A per-unit rebate cancels the tax at the margin, so the firm is back to maximizing pure profit (Q = 60). A fixed check does not depend on what the firm does, so the incentive survives.

blocks.md:
Third solution: define property rights and let the two parties contract. Gains from trade exist at every unit where the firm's marginal profit exceeds the neighbor's marginal damage, so they trade until **Q = 40**, whoever owns the right.

The professor's proof is by contradiction: any Q̃ other than Q_FB leaves a deal on the table. Ownership changes the *split*, not the output.

blocks.title: Total surplus at the efficient output = 1200
blocks.caption: Total surplus at Q = 40 is the area between MB and MD: 1/2 x 40 x 60 = 1200. How much bargaining adds depends on the starting point. If the neighbor owns the right, production starts at 0 and bargaining creates all 1200. If the firm owns the right, it starts at Q = 60 with surplus 900, so bargaining adds 300. Takeaway: either way they stop at 40 because beyond it there is nothing left to split.

blocks.title: A judge asks: who should own the right?
blocks.prompt: Marginal profit is 60 - Q and marginal damage is 0.5Q. Bargaining is free, everyone knows everything, and both sides can pay. The court can give the right to the neighbor (firm must buy permission) or to the firm (neighbor must pay it to cut back).

choices.label: Give it to the neighbor
choices.outcome: The firm buys permission up to Q = 40 and pays between 400 and 1600. At the top price the neighbor captures all 1200 of surplus and the firm gets 0.

choices.label: Give it to the firm
choices.outcome: The neighbor pays the firm to cut from 60 to 40, at a price between 200 and 500. At the top price the firm earns 2100 and the neighbor is at -900, no better than the free market.

choices.label: Neither works unless we first calculate the right tax
choices.outcome: Not so: with zero transaction costs, output is 40 either way and no damage calculation is needed. You would be doing Pigou's hard arithmetic for nothing.

blocks.debrief: Same Q = 40 under both assignments. What changes is who is rich: the owner can extract nearly all the surplus. Efficiency is untouched, distribution is not.

blocks.md:
Coase needs three things: **costless transacting, payoff-maximizing parties, and shared information.** Break any one and bargaining stops short of Q_FB. Policy then falls back to a tax or a quantity rule.

Match each case to the assumption it breaks.

blocks.prompt: Which assumption fails in each case?

items.label: Tens of thousands of people breathe the same smog
Nine years of litigation over a shared oil field (Talos and Pemex)
The neighbor owes the firm more than they can borrow
You hold a box whose contents only your friend knows; you ask $4.5 million to give it back

blocks.why: Air pollution is Coase's own example of costs too high to bargain. A wealth-constrained neighbor can't buy Q_FB when the firm owns the right, so ownership changes output. A take-it-or-leave-it offer under hidden information misses trades the low-profit type would have taken.

blocks.headline: Carbon Pricing September 2026 Update: RGGI hits a record price; California-Québec auction clears 13% higher
blocks.tieIn: California uses a quantity rule (a cap with traded permits) where South Africa chose a carbon tax in 2019. The auction price here is the market finding the 'tax' the cap implies, and RGGI's auction proceeds topped $1 billion: real revenue, and the question of who gets it.

blocks.q: Which setting is the worst fit for a Coasean bargain?
options: A factory next to one neighbor with clear titles
Two firms that know each other's costs and have cash
A landowner and tenant with a written lease
Thousands of residents downwind of one plant
blocks.why: Each resident would need a lawyer and a contract, and each could hold out. That is transaction costs at scale, so a tax or regulation fits better.

quiz.q: Marginal profit is 60 - Q and marginal damage is 0.5Q. Which tax makes the firm choose the efficient output?
options: $40, the efficient quantity
$30, marginal damage at the market output
$20, marginal damage at Q = 40
$60, the firm's top marginal profit
quiz.why: Efficient Q solves 60 - Q = 0.5Q, so Q = 40. The tax is marginal damage there: 0.5 x 40 = 20.

quiz.q: A regulator sets the tax at marginal damage at the free-market output (30) instead. What happens?
options: Output drops below 40; a deadweight loss of 75 appears
Output stays at 60 because the tax is only a transfer
Output lands exactly at 40, since any tax gets it there
Output rises because the firm earns more on each unit
quiz.why: The firm cuts to Q = 60 - 30 = 30, past the optimum. Because marginal damage is rising, the right tax is read at Q_FB, not Q_M.

quiz.q: The government rebates the tax to the firm for every unit produced. What does the firm do?
options: Produces 40, because it is still formally being taxed
Produces 0, because it is no better off than before
Produces 60, since the tax is cancelled at the margin
Produces 30, halfway between the two outputs it knows
quiz.why: Returning τ per unit means the firm's marginal condition is back to P - C' = 0. A fixed lump-sum check keeps the incentive.

quiz.q: With zero transaction costs, the court switches the right from the neighbor to the firm. What changes?
options: Output rises to 60 now that the firm owns the right
Output falls to 0 because the neighbor can block it
Who pays whom and who ends richer, but not output
Nothing at all, since payments and output both stay put
quiz.why: Coase: Q = 40 either way. The firm-owns case has the neighbor paying 200 to 500; the neighbor-owns case has the firm paying 400 to 1600.

quiz.q: Which is the best reason Coasean bargaining often fails for air pollution?
options: Firms refuse to maximize profit when asked to bargain
Too many affected people to contract with each one
Marginal damage is not increasing in output at all
The tax revenue is too large for anyone to rebate
quiz.why: Coase himself gave air pollution as the high-transaction-cost case: tens of thousands of people, each needing a deal. Regulation or a tax steps in.

flashcards.back: A cost or benefit that falls on someone who doesn't take part in the decision, so the decider ignores it.
A per-unit tax equal to marginal damage at the efficient output: τ = D′(Q_FB). It turns the externality into a cost the firm feels.

flashcards.front: Why read D′ at Q_FB, not Q_M?
flashcards.back: Marginal damage rises with output. D′(Q_M) is higher than D′(Q_FB), so taxing there overshoots and cuts output below the optimum.
R = τ·Q_FB = D′(Q_FB)·Q_FB. With the lesson's numbers: 20 x 40 = 800.
With costless transacting, payoff-maximizing parties and shared information, bargaining reaches the efficient Q however property rights are assigned.
Transaction costs, parties that can't maximize (e.g., cash constraints), and private information (no-trade results).

recap: Market output (Q_M = 60) overshoots the social optimum (Q_FB = 40); the gap costs 300 of surplus.
A Pigouvian tax equals marginal damage at Q_FB ($20), not at the market output ($30). Revenue is 800 and can be returned lump-sum, never per unit.
With zero transaction costs, bargaining finds Q = 40 under either ownership rule; ownership only moves the money.
Coase fails with transaction costs, cash constraints, or private information, which is why taxes and quotas exist.
